title: Queue splay probing scratch
content:
Objective:
Short experiments to understand whether adding a small randomized splay window when dispatching requests into the batching/queueing layer reduces extreme tail (p99/p999) under mixed-priority client traffic without materially hurting steady-state throughput.

Why this feels worth trying:
- In prior field traces we see tightly synchronized arrival groups (client-side fan-in + retries) producing micro-synchrony in the batcher that inflates p99.
- A small randomized offset on request enqueue reduces instantaneous clustering, potentially smoothing batch sizes and lowering tail.

Hypothesis:
A 5–30ms randomized splay (uniform) applied to request enqueue times will: (a) reduce p99 latency by breaking micro-clumps, (b) keep p50/p95 within 10% of baseline, and (c) not reduce aggregate tokens/sec by more than 5% for typical payload distributions.

Testbed / Setup:
- Cluster: 4 x A100-40G equivalent nodes in staging (mixed partition), 8 vCPUs control-plane runner capturing traces.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.23.1 (local build with splay flag).
- Model: open-llama-7B quantized (4-bit), seq_len=512 typical, avg_tokens_out=80.
- Workload generator: synthetic mix from real trace sampler (mix of small chat messages and long completions): 70% short (<=40 tokens), 30% long (80–256 tokens).
- Arrival patterns: two lanes: high-priority (HP) and best-effort (BE). HP = 20% of requests but tight bursts (10–30 reqs over 50ms windows every 2s). BE = Poisson baseline 200 qps.
- Key runtime knobs under test: splay-window-ms (0/5/20/100), max-inflight-per-worker (8), preemption (off/on), batching_timeout_ms=12, batch_max_tokens=4096.
- Metrics collected: qps, tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99/p999 latency (enqueue->response), batch size distribution, batch wait time, KV cache hit rate, CPU/GPU utilization.

Run summary (aggregated over 10m steady windows):
CONFIG | qps | tokens/s | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | p999 (ms) | mean batch size
0 ms splay | 245 | 57,100 | 9.8 | 42.3 | 320.6 | 610.4 | 6.3
5 ms splay | 244 | 56,800 | 10.1 | 41.9 | 235.2 | 410.7 | 5.9
20 ms splay | 239 | 55,600 | 11.4 | 43.6 | 230.1 | 398.9 | 5.1
100 ms splay | 221 | 51,800 | 15.9 | 54.2 | 480.7 | 1150.3 | 3.0

Key takeaways from the numbers above:
- Small splay windows (5–20ms) materially reduced p99 (approx 27%–28% reduction from baseline at 0 ms). p999 also improved significantly.
- p50 stayed stable (within ~15%); small increase is expected because randomizing enqueue adds tiny wait.
- Large splay (100ms) harms throughput and massively increases tail due to batching inefficiency and larger waiting windows causing resource underutilization and more context switches.

Batching behavior notes:
- With 0ms splay we saw more frequent instantaneous batch size spikes (10–20 reqs) that correlate with p99 spikes.
- 5–20ms splay reduces variance of batch size; mean batch size decreases slightly but batch utilization remained >80% for CPU/GPU kernels.
- 100ms splay causes many small batches (mean 3) and higher overhead per-token.

Interaction with preemption:
- Enabling preemption + 20ms splay improved HP p99 by additional ~15% vs splay-only, at the cost of a small BE throughput drop (~3%).
- Preemption strategy used: interrupt BE in-progress batches when HP arrival threshold exceeded; we used conservative preemption (drain after token boundary).

Oddities / anomalies observed:
- Periodic tail spikes (~every 30s) persisted across splay settings. Correlated with minor Python GC pauses on the control-plane sampler process (10–30ms), but those alone don't fully explain the 200–400ms tail jumps. Need to correlate with node-level Nvlink/PCIe interrupts and container CPU throttling events (observed on one node at ~95% GPU util).
- KV cache hit rate stayed flat (~78%) across splay values. Hypothesis: splay randomized enqueue doesn't alter cache affinity because requests are identical enough to be coalesced in time window from model's perspective.

Micro-observations from traces (single interesting window):
- 2024-10-03T14:12:22Z: HP burst of 24 requests arrives; with 0ms splay produced immediate batch of 18 + 6 in next tick -> p99 spike 480ms.
- With 20ms splay same burst distributed -> three smaller batches over 60ms window -> p99 for HP reduced to 235ms.

Conclusions (quick):
- Add a small randomized splay (5–20ms) in the enqueue path is a cheap, effective mitigation for micro-clustered arrivals that drive the tail. It trades a tiny increase in median for a significant tail win.
- Large splay windows (>50ms) start to hurt throughput and worsen tail due to under-filled batches and queuing amplification.
- Combining splay + conservative preemption is promising for mixed-priority traffic.

Next steps (prioritized):
1) Run ±scale tests on a larger cluster (8–16 nodes) to validate that small-splay improvements persist at higher qps and with multi-tenant noise.
2) Add an adaptive splay: use short-term ingress variance (sliding 1s window) to tune splay-window (0–30ms) dynamically instead of static config.
3) Correlate the periodic 30s tail spikes with node-level telemetry (dmesg, pci counters) and GC traces; add pprof sampling for the control-plane to rule out lock contention.
4) Test with different model seq lengths (short chat vs long completion) and with smaller GPU sizes (T4) to see dependency on kernel startup/overhead.
5) Draft an internal playbook with recommended defaults: splay=10ms, batching_timeout=12ms, preemption=on (conservative) for HP-sensitive tenants.
